title: GRAIN BIN RESCUE
full_story:
On Thursday, at approximately 10:21 am, the Xenia Fire Protection District was dispatched to the 200 block of South Main Street in Xenia for a report of an individual trapped inside a grain bin and buried shoulder-deep in grain.

Upon arrival, Xenia Fire Protection District personnel immediately began rescue operations.  Firefighters quickly entered the grain bin and, with assistance from local farm workers, deployed grain bin rescue tubes around the individual in an effort to stabilize and protect them from further entrapment.

Due to the complexity of the incident, additional resources were requested.  Clay County/Flora Rescue and the Marion County Grain Bin Rescue Task Force were called to the scene for mutual aid.

While awaiting the arrival of additional resources, Xenia firefighters and local farm workers continued working to stabilize the individual and the surrounding grain.  Once additional rescue personnel arrived, firefighters, and farm hands deployed additional grain bin rescue panels and equipment, including augers, while additional personnel entered the grain bin to assist with the rescue operation.

Ground operations then began to remove grain from the bin.  Multiple cuts were made into the grain bin, allowing grain to be removed by hand and through the use of machinery.  After several cuts and the removal of many bushels of grain, enough material had been removed from around the individual to allow them to successfully self-extract from the grain bin.

The individual was transported to a local hospital for further treatment.

The Xenia Fire Protection District was assisted on scene by Flora-Clay County ESDA, Clay County Ambulance, Salem Fire Protection District, Kell Fire Protection District, Iuka Fire Protection District, Centralia Fire Protection District, Patoka Fire District, Odin Fire, Orchardville Fire Protection District, Illinois State Police, Clay County Sheriff’s Department, United Medical Response, and other Fire Departments that were placed on standby, and numerous local farm workers and members of the public who provided invaluable assistance during the rescue.

Three members of the Xenia Fire Protection District and One ESDA member were also seen at a local hospital for evaluation and treatment after experiencing a reaction to grain dust and heat related issues.

Xenia Fire Chief Vince King said “the Xenia Fire Protection District would like to extend its sincere appreciation to every agency, emergency responder, farm worker, and member of the public who responded and assisted during this incident.  Grain bin rescues are extremely dangerous and complex operations that require specialized equipment, training, personnel, and teamwork.”

“Today’s successful outcome was made possible by the tremendous cooperation and dedication of everyone involved.”

“We are grateful to all who came together to help bring this individual home safely.”

title: ELM RIVER CHOWDER
full_story:
The Elm River Chowder will be held Saturday, September 5th at the Chowder Grounds.  Cost of the chowder is by donation.  Chowder will be for sale by the bowl with seating available and chowder will also be dipped by the bulk at around 12:30 pm.  Please, do not bring glass or plastic containers.

There will also be pulled pork sandwiches, nachos, hot dogs, pie by the slice or whole, and cold drinks.

The Elm River chowder grounds are either six miles south of Clay City off of Route 50 or four miles east of the Rinard Crossroads off of Route 45, watch for signs.

The Elm River Chowder is an over 100 year tradition, funded entirely by donation.  Vegetable prep will begin at 7 am, volunteers are welcome.  For more information, find the Elm River Chowder on Facebook.

title: MADAGASCAR A MUSICAL ADVENTURE
full_story:
OCC Theater is preparing to bring a wild adventure to the stage this fall with “Madagascar, A Musical Adventure!” as part of its Theatre for Young Audiences series.

Auditions are open to high school students and older and will be held at the Dr. John D. Stull Performing Arts Center on September 20th at 2 pm and September 21st at 6 pm.  Those interested in auditioning only need to attend one of the two audition sessions.

Based on the popular DreamWorks Movie, “Madagascar, A Musical Adventure!” follows some of the zoo’s most entertaining residents as they leave New York City behind.  The musical follows Alex the Lion, Marty the Zebra, Melman the Giraffe and Gloria the Hippo, along with the hilarious penguins, as they embark on an unforgettable journey from the Central Park Zoo to Madagascar.

The production is expected to bring the colorful characters, humor and adventure of the story to life for audiences of all ages.

Audition materials are available through OCC Theater at iecc.edu/occ/theater.

Following auditions and rehearsals, “Madagascar, A Musical Adventure!” is scheduled to hit the Ruth Henry Stage at the Dr. John D. Stull Performing Arts Center, at Olney Central College, November 20th through 22nd.

With familiar characters, plenty of humor and an adventure that travels from New York to the island of Madagascar, the production promises an entertaining experience for families and young theatergoers.

Those interested in auditioning are encouraged to review the audition materials and attend one of the September sessions.

title: PALESTINE RODEO
full_story:
The Palestine Rodeo is still on, according to the Palestine Chamber of Commerce, though flood waters have made it hard on campers.

According to chamber members, rising water levels from recent severe weather flooded the campground at Leaverton Park.  Due to this, camping at the park has been cancelled over Labor Day weekend.  They added that the rodeo, however, planned for the long weekend, is still going forward.

All vendors, Main Street activities, as well as the beer tent, will still be up and running as scheduled.  Chamber members apologized for any inconvenience to campers and said that they will be calling all registered campers to ensure they receive the update.

title: DUQUOIN STATE FAIR STARTS TODAY
full_story:
Fairgoers at the 2026 Du Quoin State Fair will find no shortage of free entertainment throughout the grounds.

Jerry Costello II, Director of the Illinois Department of Agriculture  said “Governor Pritzker has made affordability a priority for the Du Quoin State Fair, and our team has looked for every opportunity to deliver on that.  Admission is always free, and with a wide variety of performances and attractions available at no cost, families can enjoy a full day of fun without worrying about their wallets.”

Inside the free entertainment tent, located on the north side of the Midway, music acts for all ages entertain fairgoers looking to get out of the heat and off their feet.  This tent offers plenty of room for little ones to move around, and plenty of seating to enjoy your favorite fair food.

The Du Quoin State Fair starts today and runs through September 7th.  Admission to the fair is free, and parking is free today.  For remaining fair dates, parking is $15 for Gate 1, and $10 for all other gates.  Please visit dsf.illinois.gov for additional information.

title: HONOR FLIGHT 78
full_story:
Land of Lincoln Honor Flight will be taking Mission #78 on Tuesday from Springfield Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport.

Mission #78 will serve 92 veterans – 5 Korean and 87 Vietnam Era Veterans – from 52 Illinois home towns.

These Veterans and their Guardians will report Tuesday to the Abraham Lincoln Capitol Airport at 4:00 AM to travel to Washington DC to visit the World War II, Korean and Vietnam War Memorials, as well as Arlington National Cemetery Tomb of the Unknowns, the Lincoln Memorial, the National Air & Space Museum in Chantilly, Virginia, the US Marine Corps Memorial and the US Air Force Memorial.  This day of honor is provided at absolutely no cost to veterans and is completely funded by donations from the general public.

These 92 heroes will return to the Springfield airport at 9:30 PM Tuesday evening.  The general public, friends, family and LLHF alumni veterans are encouraged to pack the airport to welcome home these heroes.  Greeters are encouraged to arrive early and show appreciation for and support of these veterans who sacrificed so much for our country.  Parking is free and volunteers will be in the parking area to assist guests to open spaces.  A shuttle bus is available to take guests from the parking lot directly to the airport terminal door.

Any veteran who served at any time up through May 7th, 1975 is eligible to participate on an Honor Flight regardless of where they served or their assigned duties.  Any seriously impaired or terminally ill WWII, Korean era or Vietnam era veteran will be given flight priority.  Veteran and Guardian Applications may be obtained at www.LandofLincolnHonorFlight.org by clicking on “Applications” tab.  LLHF also offers a “Flightless Honor Flight” program for those otherwise eligible veterans whose physical condition limits their ability to participate on an actual flight.

Land of Lincoln Honor Flight is a 501(c)3 non-profit organization.  It is only able to honor veterans due to the generous donations, sponsorships, fundraising events, merchandise sales and supporting efforts of the many local businesses, individuals, and organizations within the service area.

title: META SETTLEMENT
full_story:
Illinois will receive up to $768 million from a multi-state $17.1 billion settlement with social media giant Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, the culmination of a three-year legal battle brought by state attorneys general.

Nearly three dozen AGs, including Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, sued Meta in 2023 over teen social media addiction, following a two-year investigation into decisions made by company executives to encourage more engagement on its social media platforms.  The lawsuits alleged engineers greenlit more addictive features like infinite scroll and autoplay despite internal company research showing the harms of compulsive social media use on teens’ brains, in addition to misleading the public about the safety of its platforms.

The settlement, announced Wednesday, abruptly ended what was supposed to be the first of several trials spawned by the AGs’ litigation.  Illinois was not one of the four states acting as plaintiffs in the federal trial kicked off last week in Oakland, California, in which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had been expected to take the witness stand.

Though the settlement still faces court approval, the $17.1 billion agreed to is one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in history.  Illinois will receive up to $768 million over a 10-year period, which will be used for youth mental health and online safety training programs.  In similar multi-state settlements with tobacco and opioid manufacturers, Illinois has used its share of settlement funds to stand up addiction recovery programs.

But the Meta settlement goes beyond money; the company agreed to strengthen its existing age verification systems for users in addition to a host of limitations for those between 13 and 18.

The settlement will also supercharge “sleep mode” to a full-on nighttime block restricting teens’ access to content feeds from 12 am to 6 am.  Muted notifications will be extended from “sleep mode” into weekdays from 8 am to 3 pm during the school year.  Meta will also implement stronger safeguards to block teens from accessing content related to eating disorders, suicide and other self-harm, in addition to restricting teens from access to so-called “beauty filters” and “like” counts.

Capitol News Illinois is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news service that distributes state government coverage to hundreds of news outlets statewide. It is funded primarily by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation.

title: TEACHER SHORTAGE
full_story:
As students return to classrooms, the number of unfilled teaching positions remains a concern at school districts around the state, but particularly in rural areas.

While notable progress has been made, the total number of teacher vacancies during the 2025-26 school year was 38% higher than in 2022 after the COVID pandemic.  And, in rural areas, vacancies were up 67% the past school year compared to 2022, according to John Glasgow, Association of Illinois Rural and Small Schools program director.

“We shouldn’t ease up our concern for this problem just because things seemed to have improved the past two years,” Glasgow told FarmWeek.  “The reality is the shortage is still a critical issue for rural schools, which feel the impact of missing educators much more severely than districts better able to absorb and redistribute needs.”

The inability of Illinois’ nearly 500 rural school districts to find and retain educators is a direct threat to students’ ability to obtain high-quality skills and knowledge, and a detriment to long-term local, social and economic vitality, according to Glasgow.

The number of unfilled positions started rising after COVID-19, when many teachers left the profession, and peaked during the 2023-24 school year.  In response, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and ISBE introduced the Teacher Vacancy Grant Pilot Program and other efforts to retain and recruit Illinois teachers.

The pilot project identified 170 districts as eligible to receive awards based on having the most unfilled teaching positions.  Of those, 60% (102) of awards were directed to rural districts and 40% (68) to urban districts.  Of 852 school districts in Illinois, more than half (500) are rural.

In its first three years, the project received a total of $120 million to support locally driven strategies to recruit and retain educators in the school districts with the greatest staffing needs, said Illinois State Superintendent of Education Tony Sanders.  No longer a pilot project, the grant program this year received $15 million, a smaller amount, but a priority in a “tight fiscal budget,” Sanders said.

Rural and small districts still find it challenging to offer competitive wages and benefits.  Geography and transportation also make it difficult to get and keep rural teachers.  Further, an earlier survey showed that school districts without a nearby interstate highway are harder to staff, Glasgow said.

Meanwhile, schools are using a variety of approaches to recruit new teachers, such as signing bonuses, housing stipends, down-payment assistance or loan repayments.  Attempts to retain current teachers include providing materials, supplies, coaching and school culture supports.

title: THYROID TABLETS RECALLED
full_story:
A thyroid medication has been recalled because there’s a possibility that it’s “superpotent.”

Vitruvias Therapeutics Inc. is voluntarily recalling one lot of thyroid tablets, USP 30 mg, because testing confirmed the product has the potential to be stronger than it should be.

According to the company, consumption of superpotent thyroid tablets can cause hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) and related negative health effects.  Older adults, pregnant women and infants are the most at risk of adverse effects from over-treating hypothyroidism.

The affected lot number is 504950, and the tablets were distributed from January 31st to September 30th, 2025, and they expire September 30th, 2026.

The company said people currently taking the medication should not stop using it without contacting their healthcare provider for further guidance and/or a replacement prescription.  The company hasn’t received any reports of adverse events known to be related to this recall.
